svg.text: THE FINANCIALS — how profit, cash-flow & balance-sheet fit together
Collectively they're "financial performance metrics" (the "fundamentals"). They fall out of THREE statements that interlock:
the income statement walks revenue to profit; the cash-flow statement ties it to cash; the balance sheet is the snapshot.
what's left after the direct cost of the product
≈ EBIT (Earnings Before Interest & Taxes) · core-business profit
Net Profit · Net Earnings · "earnings" · the "bottom line"
↓ the bottom line of the P&L becomes the starting line of the cash-flow statement (indirect method) ↓
CFO · Cash from Operations · real cash from day-to-day operations
CFO − Capex · cash left after operations and reinvestment
the accrual cost of past capex
firms. D&A hides in COGS or opex.
debt paydown, and M&A. But it
↓ those two are FLOWS over a period; the balance sheet is the SNAPSHOT they leave at period-end ↓
the balance-sheet identity — it must always balance; equity is the residual "plug"
The balance sheet is a photo
WHAT AN EQUITY ANALYST PULLS FROM THE BALANCE SHEET · formula → one-line gloss
Net debt = total debt − cash & ST investments
leverage, net of the cash cushion
Working capital = current assets − current liabilities
operating cash tied up in the business
Current ratio = CA ÷ CL · Quick = (CA − inv.) ÷ CL
liquidity — can it cover the next 12 months?
Book value / share = equity ÷ shares out
accounting net worth behind one share
leverage vs earnings power — crosses statements
can profit service the debt? — crosses statements
return on owners' capital (income ÷ balance sheet)
return on all capital at work (income ÷ balance sheet)
Balance-sheet subtotal / identity (snapshot at a point in time)
